strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: existing supervised MAS defenses require labeled malicious agents, which is often infeasible in real deployments; framing an unsupervised alternative is well motivated.

The hierarchical agent encoder (agent/neighbor/global levels) is a sensible design that is empirically validated via ablation (Figure 5), showing that combining local and global context materially improves detection.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 4 communication topologies (chain, tree, star, random), 3 attack families (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool exploitation) across multiple datasets, 3 LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B), and a scalability study up to 50 agents.

Consistent and fairly large improvements over unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) across nearly all settings, supporting the claim that domain-specific design (rather than generic GAD) is needed for MAS.
Clear method description and reasonably detailed appendix (algorithm box, hyperparameters, extended results), aiding understanding of the pipeline.
weaknesses: The corruption-guided attack simulation injects generic isotropic Gaussian noise (scaled by feature magnitude) into SentenceBERT embeddings to create pseudo-anomalies. This is a strong and largely unvalidated assumption about how real semantic attacks (deceptive prompt injection, memory poisoning) manifest in embedding space; the paper does not empirically show that this synthetic corruption resembles the embedding shifts produced by the actual attacks used in evaluation, weakening the claimed resolution of "Gap 2" (misaligned anomaly assumptions).

Despite framing BlindGuard as "competitive" with the supervised upper bound G-Safeguard, the AUC gap is often substantial (e.g., ~20-30 points lower on several PI/MA settings, and even larger relative ASR gaps in Tables 3-4), so the comparative framing in the results discussion appears somewhat optimistic relative to the actual numbers.

The evaluation protocol assumes a fixed detection budget (top-K=3 highest-risk agents flagged), which implicitly provides side information (approximate number of malicious agents) not available in genuinely unknown-attack real-world settings; sensitivity to this budget or to varying attack agent ratios is not analyzed.
The code availability statement in the abstract is empty ("The code is available at:" with no link provided in the manuscript), raising reproducibility concerns for an empirical systems paper.
No variance/statistical significance reporting across multiple runs or random seeds, despite results (especially ASR differences of a few points) being used to rank methods.

The three unsupervised baselines are generic node-level GAD methods not otherwise adapted to the MAS/text setting, so it is unclear how much of BlindGuard's advantage stems from the hierarchical architecture versus simply using LLM/topology-aware features that any competitive baseline could also exploit if similarly adapted; a stronger apples-to-apples baseline (e.g., same features into DOMINANT/PREM) would clarify the source of gains.

Generalization claims to "unknown attacks" are only tested within three known attack families and their sub-variants; true out-of-distribution or novel attack types are not evaluated, so the strength of the generalization claim is somewhat overstated relative to the evidence provided.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practical problem: the impracticality of supervised MAS defenses that require labeled malicious agents for each attack type.

The overall system design (hierarchical agent/neighbor/global encoder + corruption-guided contrastive detector + edge-pruning remediation) is a reasonable and coherent instantiation of unsupervised GAD ideas adapted to the MAS setting.

Experimental coverage is broad: four topologies (chain/tree/star/random), three attack categories (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool exploitation), multiple datasets, and multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B).

Consistent improvement over the chosen unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) across nearly all settings, and an ablation isolating the neighbor-level and global-level components supports the claimed benefit of hierarchical representations.
Scalability experiment (20/50 agents) and multi-round ASR results provide some evidence the method does not immediately break down as system size or dialogue depth grows.
weaknesses: The core corruption mechanism (isotropic random-direction Gaussian noise scaled by embedding norm) is a very generic proxy for the actual semantic nature of prompt injection, memory poisoning, or tool exploitation. The paper does not provide evidence (e.g., visualizations, distributional analysis) that this synthetic corruption resembles real attack embeddings, which is central to the paper's own stated 'Gap 2' motivation and is never convincingly closed.

The method assumes a fixed, known anomaly budget K (top-3 agents flagged) across all experiments. This is inconsistent with the paper's core claim of defending against 'entirely unknown attacks' with 'no prior knowledge,' since knowing how many agents are compromised is itself a strong form of prior knowledge; no sensitivity analysis or automatic threshold selection is presented.

Despite the framing of being competitive with the supervised upper bound, the AUC gap to G-Safeguard is often large (e.g., 15-40 points on GSM8K-PI, MA-CSQA, and several TA settings), and this gap is understated in the text (e.g., claim of 'AUC>80% in most cases' is not accurate for several rows in Table 1, such as PI-GSM8k at 59-76% and MA-CSQA at ~75-77%).

All reported baselines (DOMINANT 2019, PREM 2023, TAM 2023) are relatively dated general-purpose GAD methods not designed for text/LLM-agent graphs; no comparison to more recent or stronger anomaly-detection/LLM-specific unsupervised baselines is included, limiting confidence that the gains stem from the proposed architecture rather than baseline weakness on this new domain.

No variance, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported for any experiment, making it difficult to assess whether observed differences (particularly the smaller ones between BlindGuard and baselines in some cells) are statistically meaningful.

The ablation study only removes neighbor-level/global-level features; there is no ablation on the corruption strategy itself (e.g., varying corruption type, comparing directional noise vs. alternative synthetic anomaly generation, or comparing supervised-contrastive vs. simple binary classifier training as the paper claims to motivate but never empirically tests).

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete code link ('The code is available at:' with no URL) and by the fact that the 'unsupervised' training still requires a curated set of normal MAS interaction graphs spanning topologies/domains matching deployment, which is not trivial to obtain and whose composition is not analyzed for its effect on generalization.

The novelty of the hierarchical encoder is modest: the 'global' representation is a simple mean pooling over all agent embeddings and the 'neighbor' representation is one-hop normalized aggregation, both standard GNN/GCN-like operations rather than a substantially new architectural contribution.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important gap: existing MAS defenses (e.g., G-Safeguard) require labeled malicious agents, which is unrealistic in real deployments; the unsupervised paradigm proposed here is a meaningful and timely contribution to MAS security.

The hierarchical agent encoder (agent/neighbor/global levels) is a sensible architectural design that is empirically validated via a clear ablation study (Figure 5), showing each level contributes to detection performance.

The corruption-guided contrastive training strategy is a reasonable way to sidestep the lack of labeled anomalies, and the supervised contrastive formulation (vs. naive binary classification on synthetic labels) is well-justified conceptually.

Experimental breadth is a strong point: 4 topologies (chain/tree/star/random), 3 attack types (prompt injection, memory poisoning, tool exploitation), multiple datasets (CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K, InjecAgent, PoisonRAG), and 3 LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B), with extensive appendix tables/figures for reproducibility of trends.

Comparisons against the supervised upper bound (G-Safeguard) and several unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) are appropriately framed, and BlindGuard consistently and substantially outperforms the unsupervised baselines while approaching supervised performance in many settings.
Scalability experiments (20 and 50 agents) and generalization across topologies/LLMs strengthen the claim of practical applicability.
Code availability is stated, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The framing of the method as requiring 'no prior knowledge of attack patterns' is somewhat overstated: the corruption function (magnitude-scaled Gaussian directional noise in embedding space) itself encodes an assumption about what anomalous representations look like, and no ablation explores sensitivity to this design choice (e.g., varying noise types, alpha values, or corruption strategies) or justifies why this particular corruption models real semantic attacks well.

The remediation step assumes a fixed anomaly budget (top-K=3) is known in advance, which implicitly requires prior knowledge of the number of malicious agents — this is in tension with the 'unknown attacks / no prior knowledge' framing and is not discussed as a limitation.

No comparison against simpler unsupervised baselines beyond existing GAD methods (e.g., embedding-based outlier detection, LLM self-consistency/verification heuristics, or simple clustering on raw SentenceBERT features) that could contextualize how much of the gain comes from the specific architecture versus the general graph-based approach.

Results show meaningful performance variability across settings — e.g., BlindGuard trails PREM in some TA scenarios (Chain: 86.22 vs 89.33 AUC) and shows notably lower AUC on PI-GSM8k (~59-75%) compared to other PI datasets (~75-85%), without much discussion of why certain settings are harder or what this implies about robustness.

No variance/standard deviation or multiple-run statistics are reported for the main results, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported gains over baselines, especially in closer cases.

No evaluation against an adaptive/aware attacker who could exploit knowledge of the unsupervised contrastive detector or the fixed top-K remediation strategy, which is an important robustness consideration for a security-focused paper.
Limited discussion of computational overhead of the additional GNN training and inference pipeline relative to baseline methods, which would matter for real-world deployment claims.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: existing supervised MAS defenses require labeled malicious agents, which is unrealistic; the proposed unsupervised alternative is well-motivated and clearly scoped relative to prior work (e.g., G-Safeguard).

The method is clearly described, combining a multi-level (agent/neighbor/system) representation with a corruption-guided contrastive training objective that only needs benign interaction data; the design directly targets the two stated gaps (limited multi-level context and misaligned anomaly assumptions).

Very extensive empirical evaluation: 4 topologies, 3 attack families (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3), scalability tests up to 50 agents, and numerous appendix studies (adaptive attacks, collusion attacks, threshold-based deployment, attack-free utility check, encoder ablation, hyperparameter sensitivity).

Honest limitations and a detailed failure-case analysis showing where the semantic-alignment assumption breaks down (stealthy on-topic attacks, benign style heterogeneity), which strengthens the credibility of the empirical claims.
Demonstrates a practically relevant advantage over the supervised baseline: better generalization to an unseen attack type (Table 2), supporting the core motivation of the paper.
Reasonable complexity/runtime analysis and enough implementation detail (algorithm box, hyperparameters, optimizer settings) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The technical novelty of the hierarchical encoder is limited: it reduces to a simple ego/1-hop-mean/global-mean concatenation followed by an MLP, which is architecturally similar to existing lightweight GNNs (SGC/APPNP-style); the main innovation is largely the application of standard supervised contrastive learning with synthetic corruption to a new domain rather than a new algorithmic mechanism for anomaly detection.

Absolute detection performance is inconsistent across settings (e.g., AUC as low as 59–75 for PI-GSM8k across topologies) and remains substantially below the supervised upper bound in several settings, which tempers the "competitive with supervised" claim in the main text.

The unsupervised baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) are generic structural/attribute-based GAD methods not designed for language-based MAS graphs, making the comparison somewhat favorable to BlindGuard by construction rather than demonstrating a fundamentally more effective idea versus a matched semantic baseline.

The core detection assumption—that malicious behavior manifests as reduced semantic/contextual alignment—is shown in the paper's own failure analysis to fail against on-topic, manifold-preserving adversarial critiques, and to falsely flag stylistically atypical but benign agents; this is a nontrivial soundness concern for the central premise, only partially mitigated by robustness experiments.

Evaluation assumes knowledge of the number of compromised agents (top-K budget) in most core experiments; while a threshold-based variant is provided in the appendix, the main comparisons rely on this somewhat unrealistic oracle-budget setting, which could inflate reported AUC/ASR improvements relative to real deployments.

The corruption mechanism (isotropic-direction, magnitude-scaled Gaussian noise in embedding space) is a coarse proxy for real semantic attacks, and though the appendix defends it via an “angular margin” argument, the justification is post hoc rather than empirically validated against a wider range of stealthier real attack types beyond the three considered.

Evaluation is confined to simulated benchmarks (CSQA/MMLU/GSM8K/InjecAgent/PoisonRAG-based attacks) with a fixed small number of compromised agents (mostly 3), limiting insight into real-world, more diverse or adaptive attacker behavior beyond the appendix's illustrative examples.

strengths: Addresses a practically important gap: existing MAS defenses (e.g., G-Safeguard) require labeled malicious agents, which is unrealistic in deployment; the unsupervised paradigm proposed here is a meaningful and well-motivated reframing of the problem.

The experimental evaluation is unusually extensive for the venue: four topologies, three attack families (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Qwen3-8B), scalability tests up to 50 agents, and a large appendix of robustness checks (threshold-based deployment, collusion/sacrificial-decoy attacks, adaptive attacks, encoder-ablation controls, attack-free utility checks, and failure-case analysis).
The ablation study (RQ4) convincingly shows that combining agent-, neighbor-, and system-level information is necessary, supporting the paper's central architectural claim.

The generalization result against unseen attack types (Table 2), where the unsupervised model outperforms the supervised G-Safeguard when tested on an attack type not seen in training, is a genuinely useful and non-trivial finding that supports the paper's main motivation.

The paper is transparent about limitations (reactive rather than preventive defense, evaluation confined to simulated MAS) and provides an honest failure-case discussion showing where the method's semantic-alignment assumption breaks down.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: the components (frozen SentenceBERT features, simple mean/1-hop aggregation for 'hierarchical' encoding, directional Gaussian corruption in embedding space, and supervised contrastive loss from Khosla et al. 2020) are individually standard tools; the contribution is mainly their combination for this application rather than a new mechanism for detecting semantic/intent-level anomalies.

The corruption-based simulation of 'malicious' behavior (magnitude-scaled random directional noise) is a fairly crude proxy for actual structured semantic attacks (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning). The paper's own appendix (adaptive-attack and failure-case analyses) shows that stealthy, on-topic, semantically-aligned malicious messages evade detection, exactly the scenario one would expect if the training signal (isotropic/random corruption) does not resemble real attacker behavior.

Despite the framing of 'competitive with supervised upper bound,' BlindGuard's AUC is consistently and substantially lower than G-Safeguard's (often 75–86% vs. 98–100%), and ASR reduction is also generally weaker in the main tables; the gap is understated in the discussion of results.

The main results assume the number of compromised agents (K=3) is known a priori for detection budget and AUC computation, which is in tension with the paper's central claim of operating under fully 'unknown attacks' with no prior knowledge; the more realistic threshold-based/unknown-K variants are relegated to an appendix and show somewhat degraded performance.

The 'global' and 'neighbor' representations used in the hierarchical encoder are very simple (plain mean pooling and one-hop normalized aggregation rather than a learned multi-layer GNN), raising questions about whether the claimed 'system-level understanding' is substantially more expressive than a shallow heuristic, and about how this design would scale/perform in MAS with more complex, deep interaction chains.

Benchmark tasks (CSQA/MMLU/GSM8K-based debate rounds) are relatively simple QA settings; it is unclear how well the semantic-anomaly framing transfers to more complex, tool-using, or long-horizon MAS applications where 'normal' agent variability (e.g., differing but valid reasoning styles, as shown in the paper's own failure case) may be much larger, increasing false-positive risk in practice.
Minor presentation inconsistencies (e.g., inconsistent capitalization of baseline names across tables, a typo in Figure 2) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Addresses a practical and timely problem: existing MAS defenses (e.g., G-Safeguard) require labeled malicious agents, which is unrealistic in deployment; the unsupervised reformulation is well-motivated and clearly articulated with concrete 'gaps' relative to prior GAD work.

The hierarchical agent encoder (ego/neighbor/global) combined with directional corruption-based negatives and supervised contrastive learning is a sensible and reasonably novel adaptation of GAD techniques to the MAS setting, targeting the stated misalignment between structural-anomaly assumptions and semantic anomalies in MAS.

Extensive empirical evaluation: 4 topologies, 3 attack families (prompt injection, tool exploitation, memory poisoning), multiple LLM backbones (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3), and comparisons against both unsupervised GAD baselines and a strong supervised upper bound.

Results consistently show large improvements over generic unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) and competitive (though not superior) performance versus the supervised G-Safeguard, including a compelling cross-attack generalization result (Table 2) where BlindGuard trained on one attack type outperforms the supervised model on an unseen attack type.

The appendix contains unusually thorough robustness analyses that preempt many natural reviewer concerns: collusion/sacrificial-decoy attacks, adaptive attacks explicitly designed to evade the detector, threshold-based (vs. fixed-budget) remediation, attack-free/no-attack utility checks, an ablation isolating the learned encoder's contribution over raw SentenceBERT features, scalability to 20/50 agents, and a candid failure-case analysis discussing false positives/negatives.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility and practicality: algorithm box, complexity analysis, hyperparameter sensitivity study for the corruption scale α, and implementation details (optimizer, scheduler, hardware).
weaknesses: The core anomaly-simulation mechanism (isotropic-magnitude-scaled Gaussian noise injected into frozen SentenceBERT embeddings) is a fairly generic corruption heuristic; despite the paper's claim to model 'semantic-level' attacker deviations, the link between this synthetic corruption and actual adversarial MAS behaviors (e.g., stealthy, on-topic prompt injection) is asserted rather than rigorously justified, and the authors' own failure-case analysis confirms that on-topic, manifold-preserving attacks can evade detection.

Performance gaps relative to the supervised G-Safeguard upper bound remain substantial in several settings (e.g., GSM8K AUC ~69–76 vs. ~98–99; several tool/memory-attack topologies), somewhat tempering the 'competitive with supervised' claim made in the main text.

The hierarchical encoder itself is architecturally simple (mean-pooled global context, one-hop normalized-adjacency neighbor aggregation, MLP fusion), closer to lightweight GNN/SGC-style designs than a substantively new architecture; the main novelty lies more in problem framing and training objective than in encoder design.

Evaluation relies on a small, fixed set of unsupervised GAD baselines (DOMINANT, PREM, TAM) that were not designed for MAS text data, and the fixed-budget top-K detection protocol (K exactly matching the number of compromised agents in most tables) is somewhat idealized relative to real deployments, even though the paper does provide supplementary threshold-based and K=2 experiments to partially address this.

Some inconsistencies in presentation (e.g., 'Dominant' vs. 'DOMINANT' capitalization across tables) suggest the extensive appendix material may not have received the same level of polish as the main paper.
